summary: Loaded otsu noodles: cold soba tossed with a tahini, tamari, sweet soy, citrus and ginger dressing, tofu, grilled eggplant and cucumber, served on iceberg lettuce; vegan, serves 4 in 30 minutes, a make-ahead hit for kids and summer barbecues.
glance: 9 ounces plain buckwheat soba, about 4 minutes, rinsed cool
1/4 cup tahini, tamari, kecap manis, rice vinegar, lemon, ginger, sriracha, optional long pepper
faq: What are otsu noodles?
Cold Chinese sesame noodles include peanut butter in the sauce; otsu is really based on sesame paste. The dressing here is lively with sweet and regular soy sauce, ginger, citrus and spices.
What is long pepper?

An unusual spice with a rich history, grown primarily in Indonesia and used in Europe as early as the 5th century BC. It fell out of favor as black pepper became common. It has a floral aroma along with the heat and numbs the tongue slightly like Szechwan peppercorn; if you can't find it, use 1/2 teaspoon of black pepper.
Is it good for a party?
Yes: it's a cold dish that's a huge hit with kids as well as adults, and easy to make ahead for summer barbecues.
How should the dressing be?
Fairly liquid, not pasty, and highly flavored. Taste and adjust salt, citrus and heat, thinning with a little cool water if too thick but flavorful.
How do I prepare the eggplant and tofu?

Brush eggplant rounds with oil and grill or broil until deep brown and thoroughly tender, then cut into 2 x 1 inch pieces; dry the tofu rectangles thoroughly and saute in a single layer over high heat until browned on all sides.

summary: Chana chaat in a papadum bowl: a papadum toasted over a ramekin into a bowl, filled with chickpeas tossed in chaat masala, topped with yogurt, chili powder and cilantro, served with tamarind gel and slices of crystallized ginger; an upscale presentation of Indian street snacks, serves 4.
glance: a papadum wedge toasted in a toaster oven over a ramekin until golden and blistering
2 cups cooked, mixed with 2 tablespoons chaat masala
tamarind concentrate, boiling water, agar-agar and sugar, chilled and whisked
Vegetarian; vegan if you skip the yogurt
faq: What is chaat?

A whole family of delicious Indian snacks, served as street food or in shops that specialize in them, generally cold or at room temperature. They aren't very popular in America, though you can sometimes find a few items at a South Indian restaurant.
How do I make a papadum bowl?

Cut a papadum into a pie-shaped wedge, put it on top of a small ramekin and toast it in a toaster oven a few minutes until golden brown and blistering, occasionally and carefully applying slight pressure to form a bowl shape; leave it in the ramekin a few minutes to cool.
What is chaat masala?
A spice blend used to season chaat; use a purchased one or mix your own. Mix it with the chickpeas, optionally with diced cucumbers, potatoes or onions.
How do I make the tamarind gel?

Stir tamarind concentrate, boiling water, agar-agar powder and sugar together, adjust the sugar, chill until gelled, then whisk vigorously into a viscous liquid, which the author dots on the plate with a medicine dropper.
Where can I find good chaat?
The author mentions Udupi Palace in Bellevue, WA, and the legendary Vik Distributors in Berkeley.

summary: Citrus salad with sherry vinaigrette: arugula and mache tossed with a sharp sherry and Dijon vinaigrette, topped with blood orange (or mandarin) and grapefruit supremes and paper-thin red onion kept in ice water; vegan, serves 4, from a Kavana Men Cook event.
glance: 2 tablespoons sherry vinegar, 1/2 teaspoon Dijon, 6 tablespoons olive oil, highly seasoned
2 blood oranges or mandarins and 1 grapefruit, cut into supremes
faq: Why arugula and mache?
Two very flavorful greens with a slight bitterness that combine well with bright citrus fruit.
How do I make the onion taste sweeter?

Keep the paper-thin raw onion slices in ice cold water until just before serving: the cold keeps the sulfur compounds from being as volatile, so the onion tastes sweeter. Drain them well before plating.
How do I make the vinaigrette?

Combine the sherry vinegar and Dijon, then whisking continuously add the olive oil drop by drop at first and then in a thin stream until emulsified. Season with salt and pepper; the dressing should be highly seasoned.
How do I assemble the salad?
Chill the plates, toss the greens with the dressing, place them on a cold plate and top with the citrus and onions, then a sprinkle of sea salt and black pepper.
What are supremes?
Segments of citrus cut free of the membrane and pith.

summary: Polenta with grilled fennel, grilled apples, blue cheese and apple jus, an entree from a Kavana Men Cook event: creamy parmesan polenta (about 30 minutes) topped with grilled fennel and apple, creamy blue cheese and apple balsamic vinegar, finished with fennel pollen and flaky salt; serves 4.
glance: 1 1/4 cups polenta in 5 cups water, about 30 minutes, with 5 ounces parmesan
fennel until tender with black spots, apples until somewhat tender
6 ounces St. Agur or Blue d'Auvergne (or Cambozola, Gorgonzola dolce)
faq: Why serve it in warmed bowls?
The author's one regret was that the polenta had cooled too much by the time everything was added and got to the table. Pre-warm the bowls in a very low oven to make sure it comes out hot.
What is the two-facet trick?

The dish has two apple flavors (grilled and balsamic vinegar) and two fennel flavors (grilled and pollen). Using two facets of the same ingredient increases the depth of flavor; the dish would be fine without the vinegar and pollen but they take it up a level.
What blue cheese should I use?
The Cheese Cellar near Seattle Center suggested St. Agur or Blue d'Auvergne, both creamy and good for melting. Cambozola or Gorgonzola dolce would be good options.
What if I don't have 30 minutes?
Look for De La Estancia Argentinian cornmeal at Whole Foods or gourmet retailers: it's so finely ground it cooks in minutes and tastes great.
What do I do with leftover polenta?
Store it on an oiled cookie sheet overnight, then cut into squares and grill or pan-fry them the next day. Omit the cheeses to make the dish vegan.

summary: Arroz verde rethought: plain medium-grain rice stirred right before serving with a raw pesto-like puree of 2 cups of fresh herbs, garlic, olive oil and salt for a clean, bright, summery flavor and green color, instead of cooking the herbs and poblanos into the rice; serves 4 as a side.
glance: 2 cups lightly packed edible parts: parsley, oregano, cilantro, plus chives, rosemary, mint and dill
cook rice plain; stir in the puree and salt just before serving
faq: What is the traditional arroz verde?
Rice cooked with a puree of poblano peppers and herbs. The author finds it truly delicious and would choose it over the typical red rice at Mexican-American restaurants.
Why not cook the herbs?

The author wondered why he was boiling delicious fresh herbs for 20 minutes when their flavor is so perfect raw. He omitted the poblanos and made a pesto-like puree of herbs, garlic and a little oil, stirred into the cooked rice right before serving for a clean, bright, summery flavor and appealing green color.
Which herbs should I use?

About 2 cups of edible parts. The author and his daughter raided the garden for lots of flat-leaf parsley, oregano and cilantro and smaller amounts of chives, rosemary, mint and dill; vary according to what you have and what you're serving it with.
Can I use the stems?
Yes: because the herbs are thoroughly pureed, tenderish stems of parsley and cilantro can go in as well as the leaves.
Can I add acid?
Yes, a variation is to stir in a bit of lime or lemon juice.

summary: Roasted tomato and corn risotto: Early Girl tomatoes slow-roasted about 4 hours (350°F for 20 minutes, then 275°F), their juice saved as the cooking liquid and their oil used for the saute, then arborio rice with wine, fresh corn, Parmigiano and aged goat cheese; serves 4-6.
glance: 15 medium, roasted 20 minutes at 350°F, peeled, then about 4 hours at 275°F, draining the juice every half hour
2 cups arborio with 1 cup white wine; tomato water as the liquid, then plain simmering water
roast the tomatoes a day ahead in oil to use the tomato oil for the saute
faq: Why slow-roast tomatoes?

The author calls it alchemy: bland Early Girls are concentrated and transformed by a slow roast with olive oil. He adapted the technique from Tom Colicchio's Think Like a Chef, which devotes a chapter to roasted tomatoes.
How do I roast and peel the tomatoes?

Toss halved, cored tomatoes with oil and salt and place cut-side down on a foil-lined sheet, bake at 350°F about 20 minutes until the skins loosen, cool a few minutes and peel, then roast at 275°F for about 4 hours, pouring off and reserving the juice every half hour. Alternatively, cut an X in the bottom, blanch 30 seconds in boiling water and peel before roasting.
How does the risotto use the tomato byproducts?

The roasted tomatoes are stored in oil overnight and that oil is used for the saute, and the collected tomato juice is the cooking medium for the rice with only white wine besides, so the delicate tomato flavor is foremost.
What cheese goes in?
Parmigiano-Reggiano plus an aged, semi-soft raw goat milk cheese such as River Valley Ranch's Valley Doe. Ask your cheesemonger for an aged goat cheese if you can't find it.
When do I add the corn?

After about 16 minutes, begin checking a grain each minute; when there's a slight white pinhead that is a bit tough inside, add the corn. Within 3-10 minutes the rice should be tender with a hint of toothsomeness.

summary: Red curry fried rice with seared pineapple: pineapple chunks seared dry in a very hot pan, then onion, 2-4 tablespoons of red curry paste and 4 cups of cooked, cooled jasmine or basmati rice fried until some grains are crispy, with the pineapple stirred back in; serves 4 as a side.
glance: 4 cups cooked and cooled, ideally day-old
2 to 4 tablespoons red curry paste (leftover homemade, or check store-bought for shrimp paste)
1.5 cups chunks, seared without oil until brown spots form
Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free (check prepackaged curry paste)
faq: What rice should I use?

Thai jasmine works but the author likes basmati: the long grains fry up beautifully. Day-old rice is perfect; otherwise cook a fresh pot, spread it on a sheet pan and cool it in the refrigerator as long as possible, since steaming-hot rice is too moist outside to fry properly.
Can I use store-bought curry paste?
Yes, commercial paste can be good, but if it must be vegetarian read the label carefully because many contain shrimp paste. You can doctor it with fresh ginger for a livelier taste.
Why sear the pineapple?
A few minutes in a very hot dry pan gives at least some brown spots and intensifies the flavor, with a bit of sweetness to counterbalance the spice.
How do I get the rice crispy?
Fry it over high heat, stirring occasionally for a few minutes. It tastes best if some of the rice is allowed to get brown and crispy.
How do I cut a pineapple?

Remove the stem, stand it up and make vertical cuts along the outside to remove all the spiky bits, deep enough to get all the eyes, then cut into vertical quarters and remove the core from each as you would pare an apple.

summary: Grilled Treviso radicchio: a halved head brushed with olive oil and grilled cut-side down 2-3 minutes until seared and wilting, then dressed with aged balsamic, Parmesan shavings, toasted walnuts and flaky salt; serves 4, 5 minutes if the grill is hot.
glance: 5 minutes if you have a hot grill
moderate heat, cut side down, pressed firmly, about 2-3 minutes
aged balsamic, 12 thin Parmesan shavings, toasted walnuts
faq: What is Treviso?

A type of radicchio hugely popular in Italy and becoming easier to find at American farmer's markets. Like all radicchio it's quite bitter; the author finds a few bites invigorating but it may be too much for some.
What can I use if it's too bitter?
A milder alternative is a small head of romaine lettuce, with the coarse outer leaves removed.
How do I grill it?

Cut the head in half lengthwise straight through the stem without removing the stem, which holds it together. Brush the cut sides with olive oil and grill cut side down on a moderate grill (or a cast-iron grill pan), pressing firmly to maximize contact, about 2-3 minutes.
When should I serve it?
As a first course when you already have a grill fired up for your entrees, plain or with grilled bread for an unusual bruschetta. Cut it into bite-sized pieces and serve immediately.
What should I add?
A few toasted walnuts make a spectacular addition.

summary: Spicy mango salad with a homemade shichimi togarashi-style seasoning: mandarin zest, a toasted dried chili, toasted coriander seed, sesame seeds and salt ground together and tossed with thin ridged slices of ripe mango (cut with a serrated peeler), garnished with mint; serves 4 as a side.
glance: zest of 2 mandarins (air-dried a couple of hours if possible), 1 toasted dried chili, 2 teaspoons coriander, 1 tablespoon sesame, salt
faq: What is shichimi togarashi?

A spicy Japanese condiment of ground chili peppers with orange peel, sesame seed and other spices (nanami togarashi is very similar). The author usually buys it premade but made his own for more control and fresher flavor.
How do I make the spice mix?

Grind the mandarin zest (air-dried if you have time), toasted dried chili and toasted coriander seeds in a spice grinder or mortar and pestle to a fairly fine powder, then add toasted sesame seeds and a big pinch of salt and grind a little more, leaving the sesame partially intact.
Why no dressing?

The mango is simply tossed with the spice mix, almost like a street-food snack you might find in Southeast Asia or Mexico. Mango salads can play both a side dish and almost a salsa to eat with the main course.
How do I slice the mango?

The author used the same serrated vegetable peeler he used to peel the mango to cut thin sheets with an appealing ridged texture; a mandoline or sharp knife works too. Peeled mangos are very slippery, so use a clean dish towel for grip.
Which chili should I use?
A large dried chili of your choice; the author used aji amarillo, toasted in a dry skillet with the seeds removed.

summary: Lemon cream pasta with cauliflower: cauliflower blanched in the pasta pot, browned in butter, simmered with cream and lemon zest and juice, tossed off the heat with cavatappi and Parmigiano, and topped with buttery chili breadcrumbs, parsley and lemon wedges; serves 4 to 6.
glance: 1 large head (about 2 pounds), blanched 4 to 5 minutes, then browned 5 to 6 minutes
1 cup heavy cream, zest of 2 lemons and juice of 1, 1 cup Parmigiano
1 pound cavatappi or any short pasta with nooks
faq: How do I make it in one pot?
Blanch the cauliflower in the same pot you'll use for the pasta, scoop it out with a spider or slotted spoon, then boil the pasta right in that water, which picks up a little cauliflower flavor.
How much lemon should I use?

Plenty of zest (where the perfume is) from both lemons, and the juice of just one lemon for tang, with wedges at the table for anyone who wants more. The sauce should taste bright and lively rather than sharp.
How do I keep the cheese from clumping?

Take the pan off the burner and stir in the Parmigiano a little at a time, letting each addition melt. Cheese added to a ripping hot pan tends to clump and turn stringy. Then return to low heat and stir until the sauce thickens and coats the noodles, adding a splash of pasta water if too thick.
What pasta should I use?
One with lots of nooks: cavatappi, a corkscrew-shaped tube that holds sauce inside and out, or shells, rigatoni or fusilli.
Do I need the breadcrumbs?

The dish is lovely without them, but they add real texture. Toast panko or coarse breadcrumbs in butter with chili flakes and salt until deep golden brown, 3 to 4 minutes; go heavier on the chili for grown-ups or leave it out for a spice-averse crowd.
Where does the recipe come from?
The author and his kids first had a version at Tallulah's, a Seattle restaurant that has since closed, and he recreated it at home; it has remained a most-requested favorite.
